Today we'll be discussing a phenomenon that affects almost every large city in the world: the urban heat island.

Simply put, an urban heat island is a city area that is significantly warmer than the surrounding countryside. The difference can be several degrees. Interestingly, it's usually greatest not in the middle of the day, but at night. During the day, both the city and the countryside heat up. But after sunset, rural areas cool down quickly, while cities release the heat they've stored throughout the day, so they stay warm well into the night.

What causes this? There are several factors. The first is the materials cities are built from. Dark surfaces such as asphalt roads and roofs absorb a large proportion of the sun's energy, and materials like concrete and brick store that heat and release it slowly.

The second factor is the lack of vegetation. In the countryside, plants release water vapour through their leaves, and soil releases moisture too. This process uses energy and so has a cooling effect, much like sweating cools our bodies. In cities, where much of the ground is covered, there's far less of this cooling.

Third, the shape of the city matters. Tall buildings along narrow streets form what are called urban canyons. These trap heat, because energy reflected from one wall is simply absorbed by the building opposite, and they also reduce wind, which would otherwise carry heat away.

Finally, there's the heat produced directly by human activity, from vehicles, industry and, ironically, air conditioning units, which pump hot air out into the street.

Why does this matter? Higher temperatures increase demand for electricity for cooling. They also worsen air quality, because heat speeds up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone. Most seriously, during heatwaves, the lack of cooling at night is dangerous for health, particularly for elderly people, since the body never gets a chance to recover.

So what can cities do? One relatively simple measure is to make roofs and pavements more reflective, often just by using lighter colours. Another is to increase vegetation, through parks, street trees and green roofs. We'll look at examples of these strategies in the next session.

In today's session on the history of global trade, we'll be following a single commodity, tea, and seeing how it connected economies and shaped politics across several continents.

Tea drinking originated in China, where it had been consumed for well over a thousand years before Europeans encountered it. It reached Europe in the early seventeenth century, carried not by the British, as many people assume, but by Dutch merchants. At first, tea was an expensive luxury, sold partly as a medicine.

In Britain, tea became fashionable at court after 1662, when the Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza married King Charles the Second and brought her tea-drinking habit with her. Over the following century, demand grew enormously. However, the government taxed tea very heavily, at times well over one hundred percent. The result was widespread smuggling. By some estimates, more tea entered Britain illegally than legally. In 1784, the government finally cut the tax dramatically, and legal sales rose sharply, which demonstrates quite neatly that high taxes don't always raise more revenue.

The tea trade created a serious economic problem for Britain. China was willing to sell tea but showed little interest in buying British goods, so tea had to be paid for in silver. This drained Britain's silver reserves. The British East India Company's solution was to grow opium in India and sell it, illegally, in China, using the silver it earned to buy tea. When the Chinese government tried to stop this trade, the result was the Opium Wars of the mid-nineteenth century, which ended in Chinese defeats and forced China to open more ports to foreign trade.

At the same time, Britain was trying to break its dependence on China altogether. In the 1830s, it was confirmed that a variety of tea grew wild in Assam, in north-east India, and plantations were established there. Later, a botanist was sent to China to collect plants, seeds and knowledge about processing, which were taken to India. By the end of the nineteenth century, India and Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, had overtaken China as Britain's main suppliers.

These plantations relied on labour conditions that were often extremely harsh, which is an important part of this history that we'll return to next week.

Last time, we looked at why coral reefs are in decline. Today, I want to examine the methods scientists and conservation groups are using to restore them, and to think critically about what these methods can and can't achieve.

The most widely used technique is known as coral gardening. Small fragments are taken from healthy corals, or collected after they've broken off naturally during storms, and grown in underwater nurseries. These nurseries often look like frames or even small trees made of plastic pipe, with fragments hanging from the branches. In these protected conditions, many fast-growing species can increase in size several times within a year. The corals are then transplanted onto damaged reefs and attached using cement, cable ties or nails.

One limitation is that the fastest-growing corals, the branching types, are also some of the most vulnerable to bleaching. The slow-growing massive corals, which form the reef's solid foundation, can take decades to reach a useful size. A technique called micro-fragmentation has helped here. Researchers discovered, partly by accident, that when a massive coral is cut into very small pieces, each piece grows remarkably fast, apparently because the coral responds as though it's healing an injury. Pieces placed close together can then fuse into a single colony.

A different approach focuses on coral reproduction. Many corals reproduce during mass spawning events, when colonies release eggs and sperm into the water simultaneously, often a few nights after a full moon. Scientists collect this spawn, raise the larvae in tanks, and then release them onto damaged reef areas. This has the advantage of increasing genetic diversity, which gardening, based on copies of a few colonies, does not.

Researchers are also experimenting with what's sometimes called assisted evolution: selecting or breeding corals that are better able to tolerate heat, in the hope that restored reefs will survive future warming.

But we need to be realistic. The main problem is scale. Even the largest restoration projects cover a tiny fraction of the world's reefs, and the cost per hectare is very high. Most scientists in this field argue that restoration can buy time and protect particularly valuable sites, but it cannot replace the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. If waters keep warming, restored corals will bleach like any others.

[Notes]
Coral gardening: fragments grown in underwater (1) ______
Micro-fragmentation: helps slow-growing (2) ______ corals
Spawn usually released a few nights after a full (3) ______
Advantage of raising larvae: greater genetic (4) ______
Main limitation of restoration: (5) ______

The most widely used technique is known as coral gardening. Small fragments are taken from healthy corals, or collected after they've broken off naturally during storms, and grown in underwater nurseries. These nurseries often look like frames or even small trees made of plastic pipe, with fragments hanging from the branches. In these protected conditions, many fast-growing species can increase in size several times within a year. The corals are then transplanted onto damaged reefs and attached using cement, cable ties or nails.

One limitation is that the fastest-growing corals, the branching types, are also some of the most vulnerable to bleaching. The slow-growing massive corals, which form the reef's solid foundation, can take decades to reach a useful size. A technique called micro-fragmentation has helped here. Researchers discovered, partly by accident, that when a massive coral is cut into very small pieces, each piece grows remarkably fast, apparently because the coral responds as though it's healing an injury. Pieces placed close together can then fuse into a single colony.

A different approach focuses on coral reproduction. Many corals reproduce during mass spawning events, when colonies release eggs and sperm into the water simultaneously, often a few nights after a full moon. Scientists collect this spawn, raise the larvae in tanks, and then release them onto damaged reef areas. This has the advantage of increasing genetic diversity, which gardening, based on copies of a few colonies, does not.

Researchers are also experimenting with what's sometimes called assisted evolution: selecting or breeding corals that are better able to tolerate heat, in the hope that restored reefs will survive future warming.

But we need to be realistic. The main problem is scale. Even the largest restoration projects cover a tiny fraction of the world's reefs, and the cost per hectare is very high. Most scientists in this field argue that restoration can buy time and protect particularly valuable sites, but it cannot replace the need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. If waters keep warming, restored corals will bleach like any others.

In today's lecture, we're going to look at the body clock, or circadian rhythm, and at a particular group whose sleep has attracted a lot of research attention recently: teenagers.

Almost all living things, from bacteria to humans, have internal rhythms that follow a cycle of roughly twenty-four hours. In humans, the master clock is a tiny cluster of nerve cells in the hypothalamus, a region at the base of the brain. This clock controls many processes, including body temperature, hormone release and, of course, when we feel sleepy.

Left completely on its own, the human clock tends to run slightly longer than twenty-four hours. So it needs to be reset every day, and the most powerful signal for this is light. Light entering the eyes is detected by special cells in the retina, which send signals to the master clock. In the evening, as light fades, the clock triggers the release of a hormone called melatonin, which helps prepare the body for sleep.

This is why the use of phones and tablets late at night concerns researchers. These screens give off a lot of blue light, and blue light is particularly effective at suppressing melatonin. So using a screen just before bed can delay the feeling of sleepiness.

Now let's turn to adolescents. During puberty, the circadian rhythm naturally shifts later. Melatonin is released later in the evening, so teenagers genuinely don't feel tired until later, often around eleven o'clock or even midnight. This isn't laziness. It's biology. However, teenagers still need eight to ten hours of sleep a night. When school starts early, many of them are chronically sleep-deprived.

This has led to a debate about school start times. Several studies, particularly in the United States, have looked at schools that moved their start time later, sometimes by as little as half an hour. The results were encouraging. Students slept longer, attendance improved, and in some cases there were fewer car accidents involving young drivers.

Of course, changing school times isn't simple. It affects bus timetables, parents' working hours and after-school sports. But the research suggests that the benefits may well outweigh the costs.

Most powerful signal for resetting the clock: (2) ______
Hormone that prepares the body for sleep: (3) ______
Screens give off (4) ______ light, which delays sleepiness
Studies of later school start times: (5) ______ improved

When we talk about microplastics, most people picture the ocean. But a growing body of research suggests that soils, especially agricultural soils, may actually contain more microplastics than the oceans do. Today, I'd like to look at how plastics get into farmland and what effects they might have.

There are several pathways. One of the most significant is sewage sludge. Wastewater treatment plants are quite effective at removing microplastics from water, but those particles don't disappear. They end up in the solid material left over, the sludge, and in many countries this sludge is spread on fields as fertiliser, because it's rich in nutrients. So, ironically, the better we get at cleaning water, the more plastic may end up on land.

A second source is the thin plastic sheeting known as mulch film. Farmers lay it over the soil to keep in moisture, control weeds and warm the ground. It's very effective, but it's difficult to remove completely after harvest, and fragments are gradually ploughed into the soil, where they break down further over the years.

Third, there's wear from vehicle tyres. Tyres are made partly of synthetic rubber, and tiny particles are released as they wear down on roads. These are washed or blown into neighbouring fields.

What are the effects? Research is at an early stage, but laboratory studies have shown some worrying results. Microplastics can change the structure of soil, affecting how well it holds water. Studies on earthworms, which are essential for healthy soil, have found that high concentrations can reduce their growth. There's also evidence that some plants can take up the very smallest particles through their roots, which raises questions about whether they can enter the food chain this way.

One of the challenges for researchers is measurement. Soil is a much more complicated material than water, and separating tiny plastic particles from organic matter and minerals is difficult. Many studies use a method called spectroscopy, which identifies different types of plastic by how they absorb light. But methods vary from lab to lab, which makes comparing results difficult.

So there's an urgent need for standard methods, and for more research under realistic field conditions.

Plastic (2) ______ film is hard to remove after harvest
Particles from vehicle (3) ______ blow into fields
High concentrations may reduce the growth of (4) ______
Plastics identified using (5) ______

In our last session, we looked at how birds navigate. Today, I want to focus on a part of migration that is often overlooked: the stops along the way, and the threats migrating birds face.

Most migratory birds don't complete their journey in one flight. They stop to rest and refuel at places known as stopover sites. For many shorebirds, these sites are coastal wetlands, particularly mudflats, which at low tide expose huge numbers of worms, shellfish and other small creatures. A bird may spend several weeks at a stopover site, eating constantly to rebuild its fat reserves before the next stage.

The problem is that these sites are often concentrated in just a few places, so losing one can affect an entire population. A striking example is the Yellow Sea, between China and the Korean Peninsula. It's a vital stopover on a route used by millions of shorebirds travelling between Australia and the Arctic. Over recent decades, large areas of its mudflats have been lost to land reclamation for ports, industry and farming. Scientists have linked this loss to serious population declines in several species. Encouragingly, parts of these coastal wetlands have now been given World Heritage status, which offers some protection.

Another threat is artificial light. Many songbirds migrate at night, and bright city lights can disorientate them, drawing them towards buildings. Collisions with glass kill very large numbers of birds every year. Some cities now run "lights out" programmes, asking owners of tall buildings to switch off unnecessary lighting during peak migration periods.

How do we know all this? Traditionally, researchers relied on ringing, attaching small numbered rings to birds' legs, but most ringed birds are never found again. Now we have far better tools. Tiny tracking devices can record a bird's route, and weather radar can detect the movement of millions of birds at night, allowing scientists to forecast migration a few days ahead, rather like a weather forecast.

The key point is that migratory birds depend on a chain of sites, often in many different countries. Protecting them in one country is not enough. That's why conservation requires international cooperation and agreements between governments along each migration route.

A bird may spend several weeks at a stopover site, eating constantly to rebuild its fat reserves before the next stage.

The problem is that these sites are often concentrated in just a few places, so losing one can affect an entire population. A striking example is the Yellow Sea, between China and the Korean Peninsula. It's a vital stopover on a route used by millions of shorebirds travelling between Australia and the Arctic. Over recent decades, large areas of its mudflats have been lost to land reclamation for ports, industry and farming. Scientists have linked this loss to serious population declines in several species. Encouragingly, parts of these coastal wetlands have now been given World Heritage status, which offers some protection.

Another threat is artificial light. Many songbirds migrate at night, and bright city lights can disorientate them, drawing them towards buildings. Collisions with glass kill very large numbers of birds every year. Some cities now run "lights out" programmes, asking owners of tall buildings to switch off unnecessary lighting during peak migration periods.

In our previous session, we examined the causes of urban heat islands. Today, I'd like to look at two practical questions: how scientists measure them, and which mitigation strategies seem to work best.

Let's start with measurement, because there's an important distinction here. There are two different things we can measure: surface temperature and air temperature. Surface temperature, how hot the roofs and roads themselves are, is usually measured from satellites using thermal sensors. Satellite images produce very striking maps showing hot spots across a city. But surface temperature isn't the same as the temperature people actually experience. A dark roof may be extremely hot while the air in the street below is considerably cooler.

To measure air temperature, researchers use networks of fixed weather stations, but these are expensive and there are rarely enough of them to show differences between neighbourhoods. So many studies now use mobile measurements, attaching sensors to cars or bicycles and travelling along set routes. Some projects have even involved citizen scientists, members of the public who carry low-cost sensors.

Now, mitigation. The most effective single measure appears to be trees. Trees cool cities in two ways. First, they provide shade, preventing sunlight from reaching roads and walls. Second, they release water vapour through their leaves, which cools the surrounding air. Studies suggest that streets with plenty of trees can be several degrees cooler during the day than similar streets without them. However, trees take years to grow, and they need space, water and maintenance.

Some cities have adopted a broader strategy of linking green spaces together. The Colombian city of Medellín, for example, created a network of green corridors along roads and waterways, planting trees and plants, and has reported noticeable temperature reductions along these routes.

Another approach is cool roofs, painted with highly reflective materials. They're cheap and quick to install, and can reduce temperatures inside the buildings below. One drawback, though, is that in winter they can increase heating costs in colder climates.

Finally, water features, such as fountains and restored rivers, can provide local cooling, although their effect tends to be limited to the immediate area. The general conclusion is that no single measure is enough; cities need a combination suited to their own climate.
